chapters.title: Chapter 3: What Your ESOPs Are Really Worth

lessons.title: Listed vs Unlisted Company ESOPs: Liquidity, Buybacks and Secondary Sales

children.text: Two employees hold grants worth, on paper, exactly one crore rupees. One works at a listed company and can sell on any trading day. The other works at a startup valued at thousands of crores and may wait five years for a buyer, or never find one. Same paper number, completely different lives.

body.text: Liquidity is not a detail of your ESOP. It is most of the value. An option you cannot convert into money is a lottery ticket with an expiry date.

children.text: Listed and Unlisted: The Real Difference

body.title: Holding ESOPs in a listed vs an unlisted company

columns.label: Listed company
points: Sell on the NSE or BSE on any trading day
A public, continuous price you can check yourself
Money reaches your bank within a day or two of the sale
But you must follow trading windows and pre-clearance rules
And the price moves daily, including after you exercise

columns.label: Unlisted company
points: No market, so you sell only when the company arranges a window
Value comes from a valuation report, not a live price
Liquidity depends on a buyback, a secondary sale, an IPO or an acquisition
You may hold for years with no route to cash
And you may still owe tax at exercise long before any of it

children.text: Liquidity
is the whole difference. Everything else about an ESOP, the vesting, the exercise price, the grant size, only matters if there is eventually a buyer.

markDefs.definition: The ability to turn what you hold into cash. An asset is liquid when a willing buyer is available at a known price.

children.text: The Five Routes to Cash in an Unlisted Company

body.caption: How unlisted company employees actually get paid

cells: The company or its ESOP trust
Usually only a slice of your vested holding is eligible
Investors may prefer buying from founders and early backers
Rare, and years away when it happens
Payouts are often staged over one to two years
Fixed price and fixed window, take it or leave it

children.text: The most common of these is the
buyback
, sometimes run as a
tender offer
. The good news is that Indian startups have been doing far more of them.

markDefs.definition: A window in which the company, or a trust it funds, repurchases vested options or shares from employees.
An offer inviting employees to sell a specified quantity of their holding at a fixed price within a fixed period.

children.text: The Buyback Boom Is Real

body.title: Reported ESOP buyback value at Indian startups, US$ million

children.text: Seven Indian startups bought back close to $220 million of employee stock in the first quarter of 2026 alone, against roughly $75 million across the whole of 2025 and about $190 million in 2024. Since 2020, ESOP buybacks have put in the region of $2 billion into employees’ hands.

stats.context: The largest single buyback of the quarter, reaching more than 500 employees

stats.label: Zepto, FY 2024-25
stats.context: One of the larger rupee-denominated employee liquidity programmes of that year

stats.label: PhysicsWallah, FY 2024-25

body.text: A company that has run buybacks before is far more likely to run them again. When you are evaluating an offer, ask directly: how many liquidity events has this company run, in which years, and what share of vested options was eligible each time? A company with a track record is offering something materially better than one that has never bought back a single option.

children.text: What a Buyback Window Actually Pays You

A typical window lets you sell a capped share of your vested holding. Say you hold 10,000 vested options at an exercise price of ₹40, and the company offers to buy back up to 25% of vested options at ₹520 each.

body.caption: (₹520 minus ₹40) × 2,500 = ₹12,00,000 before tax. The remaining 7,500 vested options stay illiquid until the next window.

body.title: Size the Buyback Cheque
body.prompt: You hold 10,000 vested options at ₹40. The company will buy back 25% of vested options at ₹520. What are your net pre-tax proceeds?
body.explanation: You may sell 2,500 options. Gross ₹13,00,000, less the ₹1,00,000 exercise cost, gives ₹12,00,000 before tax. Note that 7,500 vested options remain, with no guarantee of another window.

body.text: Buyback participation is almost always capped and almost never guaranteed to repeat. Treat every window as possibly the last one, and decide how much you want to take off the table rather than assuming you can sell the rest later.

children.text: If Your Company Is Listed, Insider Trading Rules Apply to You
Employees of listed companies operate under SEBI’s Prohibition of Insider Trading Regulations, 2015. If you are a designated person, you may trade only when the
trading window
is open, which excludes periods when you could reasonably hold
UPSI
, such as the run-up to results.

markDefs.definition: The period when designated employees of a listed company are allowed to trade in its shares. It closes when they may hold unpublished price sensitive information.
Unpublished Price Sensitive Information: information about a company, not yet public, that could affect its share price if it were.

body.title: Exercising during a closed window, and other rules worth knowing

children.text: Exercising an option is not treated as trading under the insider trading regulations, except for the disclosure requirements. So you can generally exercise even when the window is shut. Selling the resulting shares is different, and the usual restrictions apply in full.
A cashless exercise is therefore a special case: because the exercise and the sale happen together,
pre-clearance
is required.

markDefs.definition: Permission from the company’s compliance officer that a designated person must obtain before trading in the company’s shares.

children.text: There is also the
contra trade

restriction, which generally stops a designated person from reversing a trade within six months. The exercise and sale of ESOP shares are exempt from it, provided you hold no UPSI, the window is open, and pre-clearance has been obtained.

markDefs.definition: An opposite transaction within six months of an earlier one, which designated persons are generally barred from doing.

children.text: None of this is optional or negotiable. Breaching it is a regulatory matter, not an internal HR one, so read your company’s code of conduct rather than relying on what a colleague tells you.

body.title: Know the Window
body.textWithBlank: A designated person at a listed company may generally exercise options even when the trading ___ is closed, but selling the resulting shares must wait until it opens.
body.explanation: Exercise is not treated as trading under the insider trading regulations, except for disclosure. The sale of shares acquired on exercise is trading in the ordinary sense, and is restricted.

body.title: Pick the Realistic Route
body.question: Sneha has 15,000 vested options in a profitable unlisted SaaS company with no IPO plan, no acquisition interest and no buyback in its five-year history. Her exercise window runs for another three years. What is the most useful thing she can do now?
options: Exercise everything immediately to start her capital gains clock
Ask the company directly what liquidity route it envisages and by when, then decide
Assume an IPO will eventually happen and wait
Resign, since unlisted options are worthless
body.explanation: Exercising ₹lakhs into an asset with no visible buyer is a real risk, and waiting passively wastes the three years she has. Asking the question in writing gives her something to plan around, and the answer itself is informative: a company with no view on employee liquidity has effectively told her what the options are worth to her.

body.title: How Much to Take Off the Table
body.scenario: Imran works at an unlisted logistics startup in Delhi and holds 24,000 vested options at a ₹35 exercise price. The company announces its second buyback, at ₹410 per option, capped at 30% of vested holdings. He has ₹18 lakh of savings, no emergency fund to speak of, and believes strongly in the company. His colleagues are split between selling the maximum and selling nothing.
body.prompt: How should he decide how much to sell?
body.modelAnswer: The maximum he can sell is 7,200 options, giving gross proceeds of 7,200 × ₹410 = ₹29,52,000, less ₹2,52,000 of exercise cost, so ₹27,00,000 before tax. The decision is not about conviction in the company, it is about concentration. His salary already depends on this company, and after this window most of his net worth would too if he sells nothing. A reasonable frame is to sell enough to cover the things he would regret not having: an emergency fund of six months of expenses, any high-interest debt, and the tax due on this transaction itself. Selling the full 30% is defensible given this is only the second window in the company’s history and the remaining 16,800 options keep him fully exposed to the upside. Selling nothing is the one choice that needs the strongest justification, because it bets both his income and his savings on a single private company with no guaranteed future window.

children.text: One Thing to Carry into Chapter 4

Listed and unlisted shares are taxed differently when you sell, with different holding period thresholds separating short term from long term gains. The exercise stage works the same way for both, but the sale stage does not. We deal with it properly in the next chapter.

cards.definition: A company-run window repurchasing vested options or shares from employees, usually capped.
Selling existing shares to an investor, often alongside a funding round.
A fixed price, fixed window offer inviting employees to sell a set quantity.
The period when designated persons at a listed company may trade its shares.
Unpublished price sensitive information, which bars you from trading while you hold it.
Compliance officer approval needed before a designated person trades, including for a cashless exercise.

points: Liquidity, not grant size, decides what an ESOP is worth to you in practice.
Listed company shares can be sold any trading day, subject to insider trading rules.
Unlisted employees depend on a buyback, a secondary sale, an IPO or an acquisition, and none of these is guaranteed.
Indian startup buybacks have grown sharply, with about $220 million in the first quarter of 2026 alone and roughly $2 billion since 2020.
Buyback windows are capped, so a 25% cap on 10,000 vested options at ₹520 with a ₹40 exercise price nets ₹12,00,000 and leaves 7,500 options illiquid.
Ask how many liquidity events a company has run before. A track record is worth more than a headline valuation.
At a listed company you can usually exercise during a closed window, but not sell. Cashless exercise needs pre-clearance.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Buyback figures are as reported in the press and can be revised. Insider trading obligations depend on your company’s code of conduct and your designation, so check with your compliance officer rather than relying on a general summary.
